processing: A gongfu black tea: as with others of its class, the leaf is withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried into fine strands. Detailed steps are little published.
harvest_season: Not well documented for this tea; as with other Chinese gongfu blacks, spring leaf makes the finest grades.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine, slender strands with a dark glossy colour.
taste_profile: Clean, with a persistent sugary, honey-like sweetness and a lasting fragrance.

brewing.notes: Treat it like a Keemun: a porcelain gaiwan, hot water and short steeps will show the aroma best.

vintage_note: Usually sold as recent-harvest tea, with no special ageing culture on record. As with other gongfu blacks, the aroma is at its best in the first year or two. Fuliang's geographical label also covers green tea, so check that you are buying the black.
description:
Fu Hong is the gongfu black tea of Fuliang county, now part of Jingdezhen in northeast Jiangxi. Fuliang is the old tea market in Bai Juyi's line about a merchant gone to buy tea, so its name carries weight well beyond this one tea.

The leaf is made in the classic gongfu way, into tight fine strands. The north and northeast of the county are the main source, and Fuliang black tea is sometimes spoken of together with Keemun.

The cup is a bright red with a lasting sugary sweetness and a clean aroma. Keep steeps short at first, and do not be surprised by similarities with Keemun.

Fuliang tea has a Chinese geographical indication, and the name is covered by the China-EU GI agreement. When you buy, look for that origin on the pack and a stated grade, as aroma claims on the label are easy to make.
history: Local accounts credit Fuliang gongfu black tea with a gold award at the 1915 Panama-Pacific exposition, a claim made for several Chinese teas. Today Fuliang tea is a national agricultural geographical indication. Little else about the origin of this style is documented in the sources used here.
